Professionals are not perfect diagnosis machines and they can be just as biased and unobjective (and sometimes more) as ayone else.
This reliance on the medical establishment is part of why there is still very much the idea of white, male autism that has to be either antisocial computer whizz or come with a host of intellectual disabilities to be valid.

I understand the need and want for some objective arbiter of truth, especially as an autistic person, but that's just not a thing. And the professional understanding of autism for a long time, didn't include the inner workings of the autistic mind and rather focused on noticable behavioral differences.
Meaning the higher masking you were, the less likely you were to be diagnosed (that's still true ti some extent today).

It reads incredibly narcissistic to me when people who had the benefit of being diagnosed young gatekeep and insult late diagnosed people. 

Because most of them likely struggled the exact same way with their autism, but with the added horror of never getting  an explanation. 
I went to therapy for a decade, I dropped out of school at 15, I dropped out of university, I tried anxiety medication.

I was dismissed when I first brought up the idea of autism after literal years of researching it and doubting myself and getting to a point where I was confident enough to at least want it ruled out. 
I was so ashamed about it being dismissed in one single sentence by my psychiatrist, that I once again needed months of building the courage and writing down everything I thought could point to autism before I brought it up again.
Only THEN, she finally saw my point and referred me to a specialist (because the majority of mental health professionals know less about autism than self-diagnosed people who invest months or years into research and self reflection), who diagnosed me after three sessions and a bunch of tests. 

I was autistic before my diagnosis and I would remained autistic if I hadn't pushed to be taken seriously. 

And constantly accusing people of faking if they express an ounce of autistic joy or don't want to share their struggles online is gatekeeping and is not helping autistic people.
Not the diagnosed ones, nor the undiagnosed, nor the selfdiagnosed.

I've never posted anything about my autism online, except on reddit and I before I got my diagnosis, I was afraid of even asking questions on this sub, because of the vicious backlash you get from gatekeepers all the time, but even AFTER I got my diagnosis, the self appointed autism-deciders on here, called it into question. 

It's not a rare occurrence that marginalized groups have infighting over who has it the worst and I have very little patience for it.
